olm8ij-f99693-d1e103.summary: Rubric naming the item 'Quaestio unica'. The single question is divided into four articles. It is a label and makes no argument.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e108.summary: Lists the four questions taken up as articles of the single quaestio: (1) whether the power to sin has free choice as its precise foundation; (2) whether the power to sin is from God; (3) from the second part of the distinction, whether all secular power and rule is from God; (4) whether obedience is a special virtue. The list sets the order of the whole item.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e141.summary: Rubric for Article 1, repeating its question: whether the power to sin has free choice as its precise foundation.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e150.summary: Opening argument for the affirmative. The power to sin requires a power that is indifferent to either side of a contradiction. A power equally open to opposites is, primarily and per se, free choice, since Aristotle (Metaphysics IX) says rational powers are for opposites. So the power to sin has free choice as its immediate foundation.
claims: The power to sin is founded on a power indifferent to contradictory alternatives.
A power that is equally open to opposites is primarily free choice.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e181.summary: Argument in the opposite direction, followed by the plan of the reply. Wherever the precise foundation of a form is found, the form is possible. So if free choice were the precise foundation of the power to sin, God, who has free choice, could sin. That is false, so free choice is not the immediate foundation. Aureol then announces that he will first state the point at issue and then set out his propositions.
claims: Where the precise foundation of a form exists, that form is possible.
God has free choice yet cannot sin.
Hence free choice alone is not the immediate foundation of the power to sin.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e206.summary: States the point at issue as a dispute among 'modern doctors'. Some hold that the power to sin is founded immediately on freedom of choice. Others reject this because of the counter-argument just given: God has free choice.
claims: Some contemporaries hold that the power to sin is immediately founded on freedom of choice.
Others reject this because God has free choice.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e226.summary: Reports two further positions. On one, the power to sin is founded on free choice not taken absolutely but as limited. On the other, it is founded on free choice as produced from nothing (or, as the text has it, 'ex corruptione').
claims: One view grounds the power to sin in free choice as limited.
Another grounds it in free choice as produced from nothing or as corruptible.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e237.summary: Transitional remark: the question has been raised to see how much truth the reported opinions contain.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e246.summary: First negative proposition: the power to sin is none of the three proposed foundations (free choice, limitation, being from nothing), whether taken singly or together. Main proof: all three are found where there is no power to sin. Those confirmed in grace while still in this life, such as the Mother of the Lord, and the blessed all have limited free choice that comes from nothing, yet cannot sin. Since a cause, when posited, at least makes its effect possible, none of these is the cause. The paragraph also includes an aside, apparently misplaced, about acts being morally good by their ordering to the end.
claims: The power to sin is not identical with free choice, limitation, or being from nothing, singly or together.
The Virgin Mary, the confirmed and the blessed have limited, created free choice but no power to sin.
Where a cause is posited, its effect is at least possible.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e296.summary: Reply to an objection. The objection says the confirmed lack the power to sin only because they are confirmed in grace. Aureol answers that grace itself is limited and from nothing. If those conditions made up the power to sin, grace would have them too, so it could not give impeccability. The conditions therefore are not what make up the power to sin.
claims: Grace is itself limited and created from nothing.
What has the supposed constitutive conditions of peccability cannot, through them, remove peccability.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e316.summary: Confirmation of the preceding reply. Whatever leaves in its subject the features that supposedly make up the power to sin cannot remove that power. Grace leaves its possessor limited, from nothing, and with a power for either alternative. So if those features made up the power to sin, grace could not remove it.
claims: Grace leaves its subject limited, from nothing, and able to choose either alternative.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e330.summary: Special proof that free choice is not the immediate power to sin. No perfection, of itself, causes an imperfection, or it would not be a pure perfection (better to have than not). Freedom of choice, in its common formal notion, is a pure perfection, otherwise it could not be attributed to God. So free choice as such does not ground the capacity to sin.
claims: No pure perfection, of itself, causes an imperfection.
Freedom of choice in its common formal notion is a pure perfection, since it is found in God.
Therefore free choice as such is not the ground of the power to sin.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e354.summary: Confirms the preceding argument by Anselm (De casu diaboli): being able to sin is neither freedom of choice nor a part of it.
claims: Being able to sin is neither freedom of choice nor part of it (Anselm).

olm8ij-f99693-d1e363.summary: Special proof that being from nothing is not what makes free choice a power to sin. Being from nothing adds only a relation of reason to the thing, because the relation expressed by 'ex' ends in non-being, and a real relation needs an actual real term. A mere relation of reason cannot give a thing a power, or make it a power, to sin.
claims: Being 'from nothing' expresses only a relation of reason.
A real relation requires an actually existing real term.
A relation of reason cannot ground a real power to sin.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e392.summary: Second argument on the same point, by dilemma. 'Being from nothing' joins being and nothingness. It cannot ground the power to sin by reason of being, or God, who has being, could sin. It cannot ground it by reason of nothingness, because nothingness posits nothing in the thing. So being from nothing is not the ground of the power to sin.
claims: Being as such cannot ground the power to sin, since God has being.
Nothingness posits nothing in a thing and so cannot ground a power.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e416.summary: Special proof that limitation is not the ground of the power to sin. The blessed and the confirmed are limited but cannot sin. Being limited does not cause a thing to be good or bad. Some divine acts toward us, such as death, are limited. Grace is a limited being and yet strengthens the will against sin. So limitation remains even where peccability is removed.
claims: Limitation is found in the blessed and confirmed, who cannot sin.
Limitation does not cause goodness or badness.
Grace is limited yet confirms the will against sin.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e445.summary: Aureol's positive proposition. The power to sin is founded immediately in freedom of choice, not taken absolutely but under two conditions: that the will is not the first rule, and that it is not of itself, by nature, conformed to the first rule. Together these two conditions make up the power to sin in an intellectual substance. He begins proving the first condition: the will can sin because it is not the first rule.
claims: The power to sin is founded immediately in freedom of choice under two conditions.
First condition: the free will is not the first rule of rectitude.
Second condition: it is not naturally conformed of itself to the first rule.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e470.summary: Proof of the first condition. A power open to contradictory alternatives that does not have, of itself, the guarantee that every act is right can sin. God's will cannot sin because it is the first rule: whatever it does is right by the very fact that it does it. Hence if God commands homicide or theft, or the killing of a son as with Abraham, or causes hatred of himself in a will, or annihilates the world and transfers dominion, it is all right. By contrast, a will that is not the first rule cannot fix rectitude in its acts by itself. It must be measured by the first rule, so it can cause an act that departs from that rule.
claims: God cannot sin because his will is the first rule of rectitude.
Whatever the divine will does, including commanding what would otherwise be homicide or theft, is right.
A will that is not the first rule cannot of itself make its acts right and so can sin.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e533.summary: Proof of the second condition. Whatever is of itself conformed to the first rule cannot sin. A created will, which is not the first rule, becomes unable to sin only through a 'weight' added to it: the grace that conforms it to the divine will. Grace is of its essence conformed to the divine will and makes one pleasing by giving that conformity. This explains why the blessed and angels cannot sin: grace, in the degree that gives perfect conformity, keeps the will set on acts that agree with the first rule. Impeccability therefore requires either being the first rule, or being essentially joined to it, or being bound to conformity by something added. The power to sin is present when none of these holds.
claims: What is of itself conformed to the first rule is impeccable.
Grace is essentially a conformity to the divine will and makes one pleasing by giving it.
The impeccability of the blessed and angels comes from grace giving perfect conformity.
Impeccability requires being the first rule, being essentially conformed to it, or being bound to it by something added.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e605.summary: Corollary: intellectual nature, considered without grace, is necessarily able to sin. Since it is not the first rule, it is open to contradictory good and bad acts. If it is to lack the power to sin, it must be fixed on the good. It cannot be fixed by itself: then it would be both undetermined and determined, which is a contradiction, and it would be the first rule. So it must be fixed by something else, namely grace.
claims: Intellectual nature without grace is necessarily peccable.
A created will cannot fix itself on the good without being the first rule.
Only grace can determine the created will to the good.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e636.summary: Raises an objection to the corollary: why should grace, rather than some other created entity, determine the will to the good?

olm8ij-f99693-d1e643.summary: Reply to the objection. An act is theologically good by its conformity to the divine will, the rule of human acts. What of itself makes an act conform to the divine will fixes it on the good. Grace does this by its proper formal notion. It is the integrity of all the virtues and includes charity, or friendship, toward God. Friendship, according to Ethics VIII, is to will and not will the same things. So grace, as a weight in the will, conforms willing to the divine will and thereby makes it right.
claims: An act is theologically good by conformity to the divine will.
Grace includes charity, understood as friendship with God.
Friendship is to will and not will the same things, so it produces conformity of wills.
Grace therefore of its proper notion fixes the will on right action.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e690.summary: Rubric for Article 2. It reads 'poena peccandi', evidently a misprint for 'potentia peccandi': whether the power to sin is from God.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e697.summary: Opening argument for the negative. Nothing evil is from God. The power to sin seems to be something evil. So the power to sin is not from God.
claims: No evil is from God.
The power to sin appears to be an evil.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e715.summary: Argument in the opposite direction, from John 19. Christ tells Pilate he would have no power over him unless it were given from above. Pilate's power was a power to sin, since it was a will to kill Christ. So the power to sin is from God.
claims: Pilate's power over Christ was given from above.
That power was a power to sin.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e734.summary: States the point at issue and reports a first opinion. It distinguishes, in the power to sin, the underlying principle that elicits the act from its defectibility. The underlying principle is from God, because the same principle elicits good and bad acts. Defectibility is not from God. It comes from the creature's being from nothing, which belongs to it of itself. God cannot give the opposite, not through any lack of divine power but because the creature cannot receive it. So God is at most a privative, not a positive, cause of defectibility.
claims: The eliciting principle of the act of sin is from God.
Defectibility comes from the creature's being from nothing, not from God.
God is at most a privative cause of creaturely defectibility.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e797.summary: Reports a second opinion. The power to sin has an absolute aspect, a positive entity from God, and a relative aspect, a relation to non-being that is not a positive entity. The question is raised to judge these ways of speaking.
claims: The absolute aspect of the power to sin is positive and from God.
Its relative aspect, directed to non-being, is no positive entity.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e815.summary: First, negative conclusion. The power to sin does not include defectibility formally and intrinsically, but only connotatively, as its term or object. A power to sin is a power for a defect as its object. The defect is not being from nothing or limitation (as shown in the previous article), and no defect belongs intrinsically to creatures from their general condition. Confirmation: in a deformed act, both the underlying act and its deformity come from a positive principle. Likewise, the principle includes defect only extrinsically, in the act, and is named from it.
claims: The power to sin includes defectibility only connotatively, as its object.
No defect belongs intrinsically to a creature from its general condition.
The principle of a sinful act is positive; defect is attributed to it only by denomination from the act.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e874.summary: Objection and reply. Objection: aptitude for sinning signifies a defectibility in free choice. Reply: aptitude for sinning is not an aptitude to fail formally and intrinsically. It is an aptitude for a defective act, extrinsically.
claims: Aptitude for sinning is an aptitude for a defective act, not an intrinsic defect.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e887.summary: Second proposition, identified as the Master's opinion: the power to sin is from God in everything it intrinsically and formally includes. Whatever a creature has formally of itself, from its nature, it has from God as efficient cause. Otherwise the creature's whole entity would not be from God. Free choice has the power to sin from its first nature, since by nature it can be either conformed or not conformed to the first rule, being neither the first rule nor conformity to it. So the power to sin is from God effectively.
claims: Whatever a creature has formally from its nature it has from God as efficient cause.
Free choice has the power to sin from its first nature.
The power to sin, in its intrinsic content, is from God (Lombard's view).

olm8ij-f99693-d1e929.summary: Second proof, by dilemma, and dismissal of the opening argument. If the power to sin were not from God, either the power itself or the aptitude for sinning would not be from God. Free choice and its power are certainly from God. The aptitude, intrinsically, is only the nature of free choice. It connotes deformity extrinsically, and only in that respect is it not from God. So everything intrinsic to the power to sin is from God. The opening argument is answered by what has been said.
claims: The nature and power of free choice are from God.
The aptitude to sin is intrinsically just the nature of free choice.
Only the extrinsically connoted deformity is not from God.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e967.summary: Rubric for Article 3: whether all secular power and rule is from God.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e976.summary: Opening argument for the negative. A relation is not caused by what does not cause its foundation. The relation of lordship and servitude is founded on the mutually consenting acts of will of masters and servants. These acts are from God only mediately, through free choice. So secular lordship is not from God.
claims: A relation is caused by whatever causes its foundation.
Lordship and servitude are founded on mutual voluntary consent.
Such acts of will are from God only mediately.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1000.summary: Argument in the opposite direction from the Apostle (Ephesians 3:15): from whom all power in heaven and on earth comes.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1008.summary: Plan of the reply: first, what 'power' (potestas) formally signifies; second, two propositions with their corollaries.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1019.summary: First proposition on the meaning of potestas. Power, lordship and servitude are relations of reason, not real relations. Aureol introduces two rival views. On the first, the will can cause a real relation, as some say of marriage, a real relation caused by mutual consent.
claims: Power, lordship and servitude are relations of reason, not real relations.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1050.summary: Second rival view: these are real relations that follow upon, but are not caused by, an act of will, as paternity follows the act of generation. Aureol doubts that any relation is real in this way except action itself. He argues against both views by dilemma. Against the first: a created will does not seem to produce anything outside itself, and a relation is produced only by producing its foundation. Otherwise, by loving someone I would cause a relation in them without causing any absolute thing in them.
claims: The only real relation consequent on an act in this way would be action itself.
A created will does not produce anything outside itself.
A relation is produced only by producing its foundation.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1098.summary: Further argument against the first view. The will is no more powerful in desiring than the intellect in apprehending. The intellect causes nothing real in its object by apprehending it, so neither does the will.
claims: The intellect causes nothing real in its object by apprehending it.
Likewise the will causes nothing real in its object by willing it.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1111.summary: Against the second view. Aureol concedes it is less unreasonable and could support the view that marriage is a real relation. Still, lordship can exist without consent, as when a ruler is deposed. Also, if such relations remained after the act had passed, dissent could not abolish lordship, since dissent cannot by itself act on a relation. Socrates' lordship over Plato would then last as long as both exist.
claims: Lordship can exist without consent of the will.
If lordship were a real relation persisting after the act, dissent could never dissolve it.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1146.summary: First principal proposition: right reason requires that there be rule (principatus) among humans. In practical matters the reason for acting is taken from the end. The end of the whole human community is to live well and act according to right reason. That end cannot be reached without a ruler. So rule is required by right reason, as are the necessary means to any end.
claims: In practical matters the reason for acting is taken from the end.
The end of the human community is to live well according to right reason.
That end cannot be attained without a ruler.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1182.summary: Explains why the ruler is necessary through the ruler's two proper acts: directing, and coercing and punishing. Directing is needed because natural light and reason are unequal among humans. The text says all can direct themselves, but the argument requires that some cannot. Those who cannot direct themselves need a superior, as in Aristotle's Politics I: those endowed with mind are suited to rule, those strong in body to obey. Coercion is needed because the human race is not wholly virtuous or a lover of truth. So penalties and laws are needed, and a superior to enforce them. Since these two acts make up rule and are necessary for the common good, natural right reason requires rule among humans.
claims: The ruler has two proper acts: directing, and coercing and punishing.
Directing is required because natural intelligence is unequally distributed.
Coercion is required because many act viciously, so laws and penalties are needed.
Natural right reason therefore requires rule and prelacy among humans.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1260.summary: Second argument: what would have existed in the state of innocence is fitting in the state of fallen nature. In innocence there would have been political rule, not rule for the ruler's own benefit. It would have involved directing but not coercing, since there would have been no vicious people or coercive positive laws. People would still have differed in natural light and talent, so the more gifted would have directed others. So rule is even more fitting now.
claims: There would have been political rule in the state of innocence.
That rule would have involved direction but not coercion.
Humans would have been unequal in talent even in innocence.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1310.summary: Corollary: some hold that if Adam had not sinned, the first-born would always have been monarch. That is false. Rule in innocence would have existed only to direct others, which belongs to those more gifted in reason. A third-born child might have been more talented and nobler than the first-born, and the others would have followed that child.
claims: Primogeniture would not have determined rule in the state of innocence.
Rule in innocence would have followed superior talent and reason.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1334.summary: Second principal proposition: right reason requires one monarch and one prince. Aureol says all jurists agree on this, following the law of nations, which is very close to natural justice. Proof from the same principle that means are measured by the end: the end of the human community, living rightly, calls for unity of rule. Multiplicity of principalities hinders justice, since wrongdoers flee to another ruler's territory.
claims: Right reason requires a single monarch over the human community.
The ius gentium, which jurists follow, is close to natural justice.
Multiple principalities hinder justice because criminals can escape jurisdiction.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1378.summary: Continues the case for a single monarch. Multiple principalities also hinder peace, since princes often rise against each other for slight or unjust reasons when no common superior exists. A prince with no superior to appeal to can become a tyrant. Where a city or community has a tyrant and no superior, the whole community may justly rise to correct him, or, if he cannot be corrected, depose him permanently.
claims: Plurality of rulers without a common superior endangers peace.
Absence of a superior permits tyranny, since there is no appeal.
A community lacking a superior may justly rise against and depose an incorrigible tyrant.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1407.summary: Qualification and application. Even if the whole community is not brought under one prince, it should be brought under several ordered in a unity, which grounds a hierarchy of monarchies. By right reason and the law of nations, when a nation fails to attain the human end because its people are vicious and everyone does as they please, a neighbouring nation that lives rightly may subject it so that it receives good living through just laws. War against such a people is even more lawful than war against those unjustly holding one's property.
claims: If not one monarch, then an ordered hierarchy of monarchies is required.
A rightly living nation may subject a nation that fails the human end, to impose just laws.
War for that purpose is more justified than war to recover unjustly held property.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1452.summary: Historical application. The Romans, zealous for justice to the point of exercising it on their own children, justly subjected other nations that departed from justice. This explains why jurists speak of imperial power. Right reason does not require that the emperor be Roman or German, only that he be the one most zealous for justice and most governed by right reason.
claims: The Roman empire was just because the Romans subjected unjust nations out of zeal for justice.
Right reason does not fix the emperor's nationality; it requires zeal for justice.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1474.summary: Objection: unity of rule hinders justice because a single prince cannot hear every case.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1483.summary: Reply: the prince can hear cases through subordinates, and when they act unjustly, appeal can be made to him.
claims: A single ruler administers justice through delegated officials, with appeal to himself.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1492.summary: Third and final conclusion: whether all secular rule is from God, not only by permission but by disposition. Universal principalities and monarchies are disposed by God, as Scripture shows: the Gloss on Ezekiel's four living creatures as four monarchies, Daniel, Ezra ('All kingdoms the Lord has given me'), 'By me kings reign', and the Apostle. Partial principalities and tyrannies need not be disposed by God immediately. Following Augustine, God governs things so as to let them act by their own motions, and human disposition suffices to provide such rulers. Of these God is more permitter than disposer, which is why prelates write 'by divine permission'. A notable kingdom that keeps strict justice may be disposed by God immediately, and when its justice fails, the kingdom may be transferred.
claims: Universal principalities and monarchies are disposed by God.
Partial principalities and tyrannies are generally from God only permissively.
God lets creatures act by their own motions (Augustine).
Kingdoms marked by rigorous justice may be immediately disposed by God, and lose divine favour when justice fails.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1564.summary: Brief statement that the opening argument has been answered by what was said. That argument rested on lordship being a relation founded on consent, which Aureol has shown to be a relation of reason.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1579.summary: Rubric for Article 4: whether obedience is a virtue.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1586.summary: Aureol sets out three conclusions without preliminary arguments: obedience is a virtue, a special virtue, and a moral virtue. Proof of the first: an act that can be performed rightly or wrongly by right reason can, when repeated, generate a habit. Subjects' acts toward superiors can be right, by keeping to the mean, or wrong, by excess or defect. Excess is rare, since reason does more than the lord commands, so that vice is unnamed. The vice of defect is named disobedience. Since the extremes are vices, the mean is a virtue, as with temperance between intemperance and boorishness.
claims: Obedience is a virtue, a special virtue, and a moral virtue.
Acts that can be done rightly or wrongly by right reason generate habits when repeated.
Obedience is the mean between an unnamed excess and the defect of disobedience.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1643.summary: Second conclusion: obedience is a special virtue under justice. Aureol distinguishes the ways justice is viewed. First, justice regards the prince in relation to subjects and requires that he know how to make laws. The virtue concerned is called positive (legislative) justice.
claims: Obedience is a special virtue contained under justice.
Justice in the prince toward subjects requires the ability to make laws.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1660.summary: Second way: justice regards subjects in relation to the prince. Some say obedience is legal justice, the habit by which a subject obeys a superior. Aureol finds this unclear. Following Ethics V, the law is an inanimate judge and the prince an animate judge. So legal justice consists in obeying not only the prince but also the law.
claims: The law is an inanimate judge and the prince an animate judge (Ethics V).
Legal justice includes obedience to law as well as to the prince.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1682.summary: Confirmation from Aristotle's Politics: as little as possible should be left to the ruler's discretion, because human wills are easily turned to evil, and as much as possible should be left to law. So the judge's precepts and the law stand in the same relation to subjects. If obedience is owed to the judge, it is equally owed to the law.
claims: Little should be left to the discretion of rulers and as much as possible to law.
Obedience is owed to law on the same grounds as to the judge.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1715.summary: Distinguishes two kinds of obedience by analogy with temperance. Common temperance is abstaining when and as one should. Special temperance is supererogatory, such as fasting. Likewise, common obedience is owed by everyone to a superior, judge and law alike. It is political and is legal justice.
claims: Temperance has a common and a supererogatory form.
Common obedience is owed by all to superiors and to law, and is legal justice.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1737.summary: Special obedience is supererogatory and is the object of a vow. Aureol concludes that obedience is a special virtue under justice. The act of justice is to render to each their own. The prince renders to subjects what is theirs, directing the good and coercing the bad, through positive law. Subjects in turn render to the prince and the law what is theirs, carrying out precepts and statutes when and as they should. This is obedience, legal justice under justice.
claims: There is a supererogatory obedience that falls under a vow.
The act of justice is to render to each their own.
Obedience renders to prince and law their due and is therefore a special virtue under justice.

olm8ij-f99693-d1e1774.summary: Third conclusion: obedience is a moral virtue, because it lies between two vicious extremes, excess and defect. Aureol postpones the full explanation to Book III, on the moral virtues. He closes Book II with a doxology to the Lord, to whom honour and obedience are due for ever.
claims: Obedience is a moral virtue as a mean between two vicious extremes.
Full treatment of the moral virtues is deferred to Book III.

olm8ij-f99693-Dd1e134.summary: Article 1 asks whether free choice is the precise foundation of the power to sin. Aureol reports contemporary views that ground peccability in free choice as such, in limited free choice, or in being from nothing. He rejects all three: the Virgin, the confirmed and the blessed have limited, created free choice without any power to sin. Freedom of choice is a pure perfection found in God. Being from nothing is only a relation of reason. Limitation does not make anything good or bad, and grace itself is limited. His positive thesis is that the power to sin is founded immediately in free choice under two conditions: the will is not the first rule of rectitude, and it is not of itself conformed to that rule. God cannot sin because his will is the first rule, so whatever it commands, even what would otherwise be homicide or theft, is right. A created will becomes impeccable only by grace, which by its nature (as charity, or friendship, which wills and refuses the same things) conforms the will to the divine will. Hence intellectual nature without grace is necessarily peccable.
claims: Free choice, limitation and being from nothing, singly or together, are not the power to sin.
The power to sin is founded in free choice insofar as it is not the first rule and not of itself conformed to the first rule.
God's will is the first rule of rectitude, so whatever it does is right.
Grace is essentially a conformity to the divine will and is the only source of creaturely impeccability.
Intellectual nature without grace is necessarily peccable.

olm8ij-f99693-Dd1e683.summary: Article 2 asks whether the power to sin is from God. The rubric's 'poena' is a misprint for 'potentia'. Against the objection that nothing evil is from God, and drawing on Christ's words to Pilate, Aureol reviews two opinions. One splits the power into a God-given principle and a defectibility arising from the creature's being from nothing. The other splits it into an absolute aspect from God and a relation to non-being. He replies with two propositions. First, the power to sin includes defect not formally or intrinsically but only connotatively, as its object or term. A power to sin is a power for a defective act, and no defect belongs intrinsically to a creature from its general condition. Second, endorsing the Master's view, everything the power to sin intrinsically includes is from God. It is simply the nature of free choice, which is neither the first rule nor conformity to it. Only the deformity it connotes extrinsically is not from God. The article builds directly on Article 1's analysis of peccability.
claims: The power to sin includes defectibility only connotatively, as its object.
No defect belongs intrinsically to a creature from its general condition.
Everything intrinsic to the power to sin is from God as efficient cause.
Only the extrinsically connoted deformity of sin is not from God.

olm8ij-f99693-Dd1e960.summary: Article 3 asks whether all secular power and rule is from God. It is a compact political treatise. The objection holds that lordship is a relation founded on consent and so only mediately from God. Aureol first argues that power, lordship and servitude are relations of reason, neither caused by the will (a created will produces nothing outside itself) nor following upon it (lordship can exist without consent, and dissent could otherwise never dissolve it). He then argues that right reason requires rule among humans, because the common end of living well needs a ruler who directs (given unequal natural talent) and coerces (given vice). Rule would have existed, as direction only, even in the state of innocence, where it would have followed merit rather than primogeniture. Right reason further requires a single monarch, or at least an ordered hierarchy of monarchies: plural sovereignties hinder justice and peace and allow tyranny, which a community without a superior may resist and depose. A rightly living nation may justly subject a lawless one, which explains Roman imperial power. The emperor should be whoever is most zealous for justice, whatever his nation. Finally, universal monarchies are disposed by God, while partial principalities and tyrannies are from God mainly by permission, though a kingdom of strict justice may be immediately disposed by God and transferred when its justice fails.
claims: Power, lordship and servitude are relations of reason.
Right reason requires rule among humans for directing and coercing.
Political rule would have existed in the state of innocence, based on talent rather than birth order.
Right reason requires a single monarch or an ordered hierarchy of monarchies.
A community without a superior may depose an incorrigible tyrant.
A just nation may subject a lawless one to impose good laws; this justifies Roman imperial power.
Universal monarchies are disposed by God; partial principalities and tyrannies are mainly permitted.

olm8ij-f99693-Dd1e1572.summary: Article 4 asks whether obedience is a virtue. Without preliminary arguments, Aureol argues that obedience is a virtue, a special virtue under justice, and a moral virtue. It is a habit formed by acts that keep the mean between an unnamed excess and the defect of disobedience. Aureol relates it to legal justice, which concerns subjects in relation to the prince. Since law is an inanimate judge and should be given as much as possible, obedience is owed to law as well as to the prince. By analogy with common and supererogatory temperance, he distinguishes a common, political obedience owed by all (legal justice) from a special, supererogatory obedience under vow. Obedience is under justice because it renders to prince and law their due, the execution of precepts and statutes, just as the prince renders to subjects direction and coercion. It is a moral virtue as a mean between extremes, a point deferred to Book III. The article closes Book II with a doxology.
claims: Obedience is a virtue, a special virtue under justice, and a moral virtue.
Obedience is owed to law as well as to the prince.
There is a common political obedience (legal justice) and a supererogatory obedience under vow.
Obedience renders to prince and law what is due to them.

olm8ij-f99693.summary: The single question of Aureol's commentary on Book II, Distinction 44 has four articles, following Lombard's text on the power to sin and on secular power and obedience. Articles 1 and 2 give a theory of peccability. The power to sin is not free choice as such, nor limitation, nor being from nothing. It is free choice insofar as it is neither the first rule of rectitude, a role that belongs to the divine will alone, whose every act is right, nor of itself conformed to that rule. Only grace, as charity conforming the created will to God's, makes a creature impeccable. Everything intrinsic to this power is from God, since defect enters only connotatively, as the object of the power. Articles 3 and 4 turn to politics. Power and lordship are relations of reason. Right reason requires rule among humans, for direction and coercion, and would have required it even in innocence. It also favours a single monarch or an ordered hierarchy of monarchies, justifies resisting tyranny and Roman imperial rule, and sees universal monarchies as disposed by God and lesser rule as permitted. Obedience, owed to law as well as to rulers, is a special moral virtue under justice. The question closes Book II.
claims: The power to sin is founded in a free will that is not the first rule and is not of itself conformed to it.
The divine will is the first rule of rectitude.
Grace alone makes the created will impeccable by conforming it to the divine will.
Everything intrinsic to the power to sin is from God; defect is only connoted.
Political power is a relation of reason, yet rule is required by right reason.
Right reason favours universal monarchy; universal monarchies are disposed by God.
Obedience is a special moral virtue under justice, owed to law as well as to princes.
